title: What Would Happen If a Black Hole Split in Two? Physicists Say It Might Look Like a Pair of Pants
excerpt: Physicists explore whether black holes could split in two, revealing a bizarre loophole in gravity.
content:
Astronomers routinely watch black holes crash together, sending gravitational ripples across the cosmos as two cosmic monsters fuse into one. But can one black hole split into two?

A single black hole spontaneously splitting into two smaller ones should violate the fundamental laws of physics. Yet a new study published in Physical Review D may have found a loophole.

Under extreme conditions, a rapidly spinning black hole or one governed by hidden dimensions of space might divide its boundary into a branching shape that physicists call a “pair-of-pants” topology.

Think of a spacetime diagram as a map where time flows vertically from top to bottom. If you trace the outer edge of a single black hole downward, it resembles a solid tube — much like the waistband of a pair of trousers. If that boundary pinches and divides, it branches into two separate tubes moving downward, so one unified black hole could theoretically split into two distinct offspring as time progresses.

“In our study, we investigate which physical laws normally prevent a black hole from splitting into two. We also investigate if certain circumstances may allow a split to happen,” says co-author Francesco Sannino, a professor of physics at the University of Naples Federico II and the Quantum Field Theory Center at the University of Southern Denmark.

Why a Black Hole Shouldn’t Split in Two

Why don’t black holes simply snap in half? The primary roadblock comes from thermodynamics and a rule formulated by Stephen Hawking in 1971. Hawking’s area theorem states that the surface area of a black hole’s event horizon — its outer boundary of no return — can never shrink. There’s no such thing as dieting for a black hole; it can only enlarge its mass.

Last year, researchers analyzing the GW250114 gravitational-wave collision confirmed this law with unprecedented precision, watching two colliding black holes form a merged horizon larger than the sum of its parts.

In physics, a black hole’s surface area directly measures its entropy — the number of microscopic ways a system can arrange its insides while looking identical from the outside. Under Albert Einstein’s general relativity, the horizon area of a standard, non-rotating black hole scales with the square of its mass. If a stationary black hole splits into two smaller pieces, the combined surface area of the fragments would be smaller than the original. Because the universe demands that total entropy increase or stay the same, a stationary black hole stays whole.

×

But the new study suggests this is not necessarily an ironclad rule. Their loophole lies in a black hole’s rotation. A spinning black hole packs less entropy — and a smaller horizon area — than a stationary black hole of the exact same mass. If a spinning black hole divides and converts its internal spin into the orbital motion of two receding fragments, the combined entropy of the two smaller black holes can match or exceed the original.

Through time, the dividing event horizon traces a single trunk branching into “two trouser legs”.

Still, satisfying the entropy budget solves only half the problem. Gravity pulls the newly formed twins fiercely toward one another. The fragments need enough outward momentum and energy to escape each other’s grip.

“But the two resulting black holes must also be able to separate rather than immediately fall back together. When we include this requirement, the window largely closes again, except possibly for black holes rotating close to their maximum possible rate,” says Francesco Sannino.

Even there, the calculation does not overturn the classical theorem barring genuine horizon splits under ordinary conditions.

Stranger Ways to Break a Black Hole

The researchers also explored versions of gravity beyond the familiar three dimensions of space and one of time.

In some higher-dimensional models, gravity allows elongated objects called black strings. These can develop bulges joined by increasingly thin necks, rather like beads forming along a stretched thread. A 2010 computer simulation showed such an instability cascading toward a pinch-off.

The researchers also explored what might happen if Einstein’s theory of gravity doesn’t tell the whole story. In some alternative theories, the rules governing a black hole’s entropy change. Under Einstein’s theory, splitting a black hole would reduce its total entropy, making the process thermodynamically forbidden. But with different rules, a black hole might actually gain entropy by shedding a much smaller black hole.

How much smaller? In one theoretical example, the researchers considered a black hole ten times the mass of the Sun. Their calculations showed that producing a second black hole weighing about 20 billion kilograms could increase the total entropy. That sounds enormous, but it’s a tiny fraction of the original black hole’s mass.

The researchers investigated another possibility involving black holes with distorted outer boundaries, or event horizons. Under certain conditions, swirling structures called vortices can form in unusual types of matter surrounding a black hole, changing the shape of its horizon. These distortions also affect its entropy, potentially making it favorable for the black hole to split into two.

A different scenario involves a spinning black hole that amplifies radiation passing nearby, drawing energy from its rotation. If that radiation becomes trapped, it could grow more intense and potentially concentrate enough energy in one place to form another black hole. In this case, the original black hole wouldn’t actually split. Instead, it might effectively create a companion from energy extracted from its own spin.

These are all just theoretical scenarios of what might happen under alternative theories of gravity and unusual physical conditions. But finding a mathematical loophole doesn’t mean nature actually employs it.

The best way to test such things is to observe the cosmos. No one has found evidence of a black hole splitting into two so far.

If black-hole fragments exist, they might reveal themselves indirectly. Very small black holes should lose mass through Hawking radiation, a predicted quantum effect that becomes more intense as a black hole gets lighter. Some fragments could potentially release detectable gamma rays.

Sannino and colleagues previously examined that possibility in a 2025 paper on hypothetical black-hole “morsels” produced during mergers. The physicists suggest that instruments such as the Fermi-LAT gamma-ray instrument might search for such signals.

The most intriguing targets may be primordial black holes, hypothetical small black holes that could have formed in the early universe. They remain unconfirmed, as does Hawking radiation from black holes.

“We cannot yet give a single probability for a black hole to split,” Sannino said. “It depends on how gravity behaves beyond Einstein’s theory, and we are working to quantify this.”

For now, black holes remain far better known for joining together than coming apart. But if astronomers ever catch one shedding a smaller cousin, it could be a clue that Einstein theory of gravity needs revising.
